findings.title: Landing safety note omits 'not a sandbox' and leaves the reader to decide which submissions are 'untrusted'
findings.quote: The tracer executes guest programs. Use trusted programs locally; hosted untrusted submissions require the separate [runner contract](RUNNER_CONTRACT.md).
findings.problem: The landing page's only safety statement never says that the tracer does not sandbox guest code, and it requires isolation only for 'hosted untrusted' submissions. The runner contract tells hosts to 'Treat hosted student submissions as malicious by default', and README states '**The tracer does not sandbox programs.**' An integrator or instructor who hosts an autograder for their own course could reasonably decide that their students' submissions are not 'untrusted' and run them without whole-job isolation. The page also does not say that tracing budgets and FIELDS inspection are not an isolation boundary. Integrators have no row in the 'Choose your path' table for hosting; the topic appears only in this sentence.

evidence.ref: cd $(mktemp -d); printf a Main.java whose main calls java.nio.file.Files.writeString(Path.of("guest-wrote-this.txt"), "x") and prints System.getenv("HOME") != null; java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Main.java --format modern > trace.json
evidence.detail: Exit 0. guest-wrote-this.txt appeared in the working directory, and the final step's stdout was 'true\n'. Guest code can write files and read the environment with the tracer user's permissions, so nothing is sandboxed.

'Treat hosted student submissions as malicious by default. Isolate the whole job ... Tracing limits and `FIELDS` inspection are useful controls inside that boundary; they are not the boundary itself.'
'Trusted local examples can run directly. **The tracer does not sandbox programs.** Hosted student submissions require whole-job isolation' (the other entry page is stronger than docs/index.md).

findings.fix: Fold a concise 'The tracer is not a sandbox' statement and host-student-submissions route into F29-3's docs/index.md/sidebar change. Link the runner contract; keep its whole-job isolation details normative there.

findings.title: JSON-consumer row starts single-trace integrators in the NDJSON batch tutorial
findings.quote: | Consume JSON or process jobs | [Batch tutorial](tutorials/batch-jobs.md) | [JSON output](reference/output.md), [batch protocol](reference/batch.md), [bounded results](BOUNDED_TRACING.md) |
findings.problem: This row combines two integration paths that have different result contracts. An integrator who consumes JSON from one `trace` invocation per program has to handle the single-command exit statuses (0/1/2/3), the fact that ordinary mode writes no JSON when a budget stops it, and the envelope rule that omitted limits are unlimited. The row instead sends them to an NDJSON batch tutorial whose clients use per-job statuses. The exit-status table and the envelope recipe are reachable only from the 'Trace your own program' row.

evidence.detail: The single-trace exit-status table ends with 'Batch clients should use the [batch protocol's per-job statuses](batch.md), not this single-command table.' The two consumers follow different contracts.

The single-trace consumer recipe ('If a budget stops it, the command exits with code `3` and writes no trace JSON. Use `--result-envelope` ... Envelope mode leaves omitted limits unlimited') is not linked from row 19.

findings.fix: Split the row. 'Consume JSON from single traces' should start at Read a trace or the tracing guide's 'Keep partial results when a budget stops tracing' recipe, then read JSON output, CLI exit statuses (reference/cli.md#exit-statuses), and bounded results. 'Process many jobs' should keep the batch tutorial, then batch protocol and bounded results.

findings.title: Release users are told to use matching docs, but the 4.1.0 first trace needs a checkout
findings.quote: Continue with [your first trace](docs/tutorials/first-trace.md), which creates its own Java example and needs no source checkout. Use the documentation version matching your downloaded release; `/next/` describes development builds.
findings.problem: The 'Run a release' path sends readers to the latest stable release, v4.1.0, then tells them to use the documentation for that release. The documentation for 4.1.0 has a first-trace tutorial that does not create its own example. It requires building from a repository checkout and running target/code-tracer-jar-with-dependencies.jar on examples/example0/Driver.java. That contradicts the README's 'needs no source checkout'. The README's relative links render the main-branch (development, /next/) pages without saying so. A reader who follows those links gets a different problem: the linked installation checkpoint expects --version to show a source commit and Java runtime details, but the 4.1.0 JAR prints only '4.1.0'. Either way, a release user meets instructions that do not match the JAR they downloaded.

evidence.detail: latestVersion is "4.1.0" at docsUrl /cs1302-tracer/4.1.0/. 'current' is labeled 'Development (main)' with docsPath 'next' and banner 'unreleased'.

The 4.1.0 tutorial says 'After [building the project](../guides/installation.md), run this trusted example from the repository root:' followed by 'java -jar target/code-tracer-jar-with-dependencies.jar trace -i examples/example0/Driver.java ...'.

evidence.ref: curl -sL https://cs1302uga.github.io/cs1302-tracer/4.1.0/tutorials/first-trace/ (and /next/tutorials/first-trace/), HTML tags stripped and searched
evidence.detail: The live 4.1.0 page contains 'After building' and 'jar-with-dependencies'. The /next/ page instead contains 'Choose your working directory'. Both pages returned HTTP 200.

evidence.detail: The assets are code-tracer.jar and cs1302-tracer-4.1.0.jar only: no source tree and no binary archive.

Prints only '4.1.0'. The source agrees: git show v4.1.0:src/main/java/cs1302/tracer/internal/App.java:74-83 is a version provider that returns only the version property. The linked development checkpoint (docs/guides/installation.md:309-310) requires 'the same tracer version, source commit, and Java runtime details'.

evidence.detail: exit=0; format=modern, entryFile=Main.java, final stdout '7\n'. The linked development tutorial does work with the 4.1.0 JAR. The contradiction comes from the version-matching advice, not from the tutorial.

findings.fix: Rewrite lines 23-26 to make the version routing explicit. Say that README links show the development documentation (the same as /next/). Link the documentation site's version menu for release-matched guides. For example, link the /next/ first-trace and note that it works with the 4.1.0 code-tracer.jar, or say that the 4.1.0 tutorial runs from a source build. findings.title: Required JAVA_HOME selection gives no way to find the JDK root; checkpoint fails for PATH-only setups
findings.quote:
Find the directory of an already installed full stable JDK 21 or later. It must
contain both `bin/java` and `bin/javac` (`java.exe` and `javac.exe` on Windows).
findings.problem: The page makes the selection step mandatory when JAVA_HOME is unset: "Missing commands or an unset `JAVA_HOME` are reasons to complete the selection step below". The checkpoint's first command also hard-codes `$JAVA_HOME/bin/java`. Yet the page never says how to find the JDK root directory. Inspection (`type -a java`, `where java`) shows /usr/bin/java, a version-manager shim, or a symlink, not the root. A reader whose JDK works from PATH alone, which the tracer supports, cannot finish the checkpoint without already knowing the install path. Novice readers following the first-trace path get stuck here.

evidence.ref: env -u JAVA_HOME bash --noprofile --norc -c '"$JAVA_HOME/bin/java" -jar code-tracer.jar --version; java -jar code-tracer.jar --version' (in an extracted code-tracer-bin.tar.gz)
evidence.detail: The first command fails with "bash: /bin/java: No such file or directory" (exit 127). The bare `java -jar code-tracer.jar --version` exits 0 and prints the version report, so the tracer works with PATH-only selection while the documented checkpoint fails.
select() falls back to searching PATH for java and javac when JAVA_HOME is empty, so PATH-only selection is supported.
The repository's own docs check finds the JDK root with `java -XshowSettings:properties -version` and the java.home property. The guide gives readers no such step.
Prints `java.home = /opt/homebrew/Cellar/openjdk@21/21.0.12.1/libexec/openjdk.jdk/Contents/Home`, the exact value the selection step needs.

evidence.ref: grep -rn "XshowSettings\|java_home\|java\.home\|JDK root" docs/guides docs/tutorials docs/reference README.md docs/index.md
evidence.detail: Only installation.md:71-72 ("Use the JDK root...") matches, and it gives no discovery method. No page explains how to find the root.

findings.fix: In "Select an installed JDK for this terminal session", add a short per-shell step to find the root. For example: Bash `java -XshowSettings:properties -version 2>&1 | grep 'java.home'` (valid when that `java` is the intended stable JDK 21 or later), macOS `/usr/libexec/java_home -V`, and the PowerShell and Command Prompt equivalents. Also tell readers to use the printed path as JAVA_HOME. Alternatively, state that readers whose bare `java`/`javac` already pass "Verify the selected tools" may use the reported java.home as the selection value.

findings.title: Text-editor checkpoint prepares learners for the \n escape only, not = or Windows \r\n
findings.quote:
Open that file in a text editor and check these three things:

1. The root has `"format": "modern"` and `"entryFile": "Main.java"`.
2. The `sources` map contains `Main.java`, and `steps` is a nonempty array.
3. The final captured `stdout` contains `7` followed by a newline, displayed as
   an escaped newline in the JSON string.
findings.problem: The tutorial asks a learner with no JSON tool to read raw trace.json in a text editor, and it explains only one JSON escape: the newline. In the modern format, `=` in the program source is written as `=`. That text is on line 2 of the file (the first thing the learner sees, in `code`) and again in the `sources` entry for Main.java, which check 2 asks them to find. A learner reading `int value = 7;` can reasonably think the source was altered or corrupted. The next lesson repeats the problem by stating that `sources` "contains the submitted source". On Windows, a shell this page explicitly supports, the guest's println output is captured as `7\r\n` rather than the single escaped newline described in check 3. This does not stop the learner from completing the checks, but it adds avoidable doubt at the first checkpoint.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -i Main.java --all-breakpoints --format modern --pretty > trace.json; sed -n 2p trace.json; grep -n -o '"Main.java": "[^"]\{0,90\}' trace.json

evidence.detail: The PRETTY_GSON and COMPACT_GSON builders for modern output do not call disableHtmlEscaping(). Gson's default HTML-safe escaping therefore writes =, <, >, &, and ' as =, <, >, &, and '. PyTutorSerializer.java:76 calls .disableHtmlEscaping(), which is why Python Tutor output shows the literal characters.

The guest JVM options are only `-Djava.awt.headless=true -classpath ...`; no line.separator is set anywhere in src/main/java (checked with grep). Captured bytes are decoded without newline normalization (StreamDrainer.java:443, OutputSlice.java:189). On Windows, println output is therefore stored as `7\r\n`.
The next lesson says "The `sources` map contains the submitted source" and sends the learner back to the same raw text, which shows =.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Main.java --all-breakpoints --format modern --pretty > trace.json; grep -c 'u003d' trace.json
evidence.detail: Prints 2. sources[Main.java] contains `int value = 7;`, `Box box = new Box();`, and `int answer = box.value;`. The root code field has the same escapes.
The Python Tutor serializer calls disableHtmlEscaping(), so the two formats differ.

findings.fix: Explain JSON string escapes for text-editor readers: modern output can encode = as \u003d, < as \u003c, > as \u003e, & as \u0026, and apostrophe as \u0027. Show escaped newline and Windows CRLF examples without implying the decoded source changes.

findings.title: Default main-exit capture fails with an internal error when main ends via a JDK-thrown exception
findings.quote: The final-state command omits breakpoint options, so it selects main exit. ... Omitted guest input is an empty stream, so reads reach end-of-input instead of prompting the tracer's terminal.
findings.problem: The guide teaches the no-option main-exit command first and says omitted input just reaches end-of-input. Suppose a reader runs the guide's own Greeting.java with that command and no guest input, so Scanner.nextLine throws NoSuchElementException. The ordinary CLI then exits 1 with an internal NullPointerException message and writes no JSON. The same happens for any program whose main ends with an uncaught exception thrown inside JDK code, such as Integer.parseInt("nope"). With --all-breakpoints the same program traces with exit 0 and records the exception in stderr. The reader gets an unexplained crash instead of a trace of the failure. This also contradicts cli.md's exit-status row: '0 ... An ordinary trace can still record an exception thrown by the guest program.'

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -i Greeting.java --format modern --pretty > gn.json (Greeting.java from tracing.md lines 85-93, no --stdin)

Exit-status table promises status 0 with the guest exception recorded in the trace.

findings.title: Neighbor-discovery sentence misstates when on-disk sources are compiled
findings.quote:
Trusted file-based compilation can discover neighboring source dependencies from
the inferred source root. In `FIELDS` mode and multithread capture, include every
required source in the submitted bundle; neighboring discovery is disabled.
findings.problem: The sentence sits in the stdin-bundle recipe and says only file-based compilation discovers neighbors. Readers will misread it in two ways. (1) Bundles piped through stdin, as this section instructs, also discover sources. If the bundle declares a package, the tracer searches the working directory, src/main/java and src for that package directory. A bundle that omits a file therefore traces successfully against stale code from the reader's working directory, and that code does not appear in `sources`. (2) The 'inferred source root' exists only when the entry file declares a package whose directories match its path. A default-package `-i Main.java` with Helper.java beside it fails to compile ('cannot find symbol'). A CS1302 reader would reasonably expect the opposite in both cases. batch.md already documents the working-directory behavior for batch jobs.

evidence.detail: findSourceRoot returns empty for no package (273-275). With an input path, the parent directories must match the package. Without an input path (stdin), it searches '.', 'src/main/java', 'src' (299).
CLI profile uses NEIGHBORS_OR_COMPILED under TRUSTED, regardless of whether source came from -i or stdin. FIELDS or multithread gives SUBMITTED_ONLY.

evidence.ref: printf '// --- demo/Main.java ---\npackage demo;\n...System.out.println(Extra.value());...' > sub4.txt; mkdir demo; (demo/Extra.java returns 7); java -jar code-tracer.jar trace --format modern < sub4.txt
evidence.detail: Exit 0. sources == ['demo/Main.java']; stdout '7\n'. Extra.java was silently compiled from the working directory.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -i dp/Main2.java --format modern (default package, dp/Helper2.java beside it)
evidence.detail: Exit 1. 'Compilation of provided Java source code failed ... error: cannot find symbol System.out.println(Helper2.answer());'
Batch reference documents that packaged sources discover roots in the working directory, src/main/java, or src. The CLI guide does not.
findSourceRoot returns Optional.empty() when there is no package declaration, and requires the parent directories to match the package segments.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -i flat/Main.java --all-breakpoints --format modern  (flat/Helper.java beside it, no package)
evidence.detail: Exit 1: "Main.java:3: error: cannot find symbol ... symbol: variable Helper".

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -i proj/src/demo/Main.java --all-breakpoints --format modern  (package demo; Helper.java beside it)
evidence.detail: Exit 0 with stdout "42\n". Step files include demo/Helper.java, but the `sources` keys are ['demo/Main.java'] only. Python Tutor output is the same.
"packaged batch sources can also discover matching source roots". The tracing guide omits the packaged condition.
"Discovered dependencies outside the submitted bundle are not included in `sources`."

findings.fix: Rewrite the paragraph. Under TRUSTED inspection the CLI discovers neighboring sources only for packaged entry files. With -i, the root is the directory above the matching package path. For stdin input, the tracer searches its working directory, src/main/java and src for the package directory. Default-package programs get no discovery, so submit every file in a bundle. Recommend running stdin bundles from a directory without matching package folders, or using FIELDS for self-contained jobs. Define 'TRUSTED' and 'FIELDS' at first use or link to the inspection section.

findings.title: Budgets section never shows how to raise a limit or use --unlimited for a complete trace
findings.quote:
Ordinary tracing uses finite default budgets. If a budget stops it, the command
exits with code `3` and writes no trace JSON. ... The
[CLI reference](../reference/cli.md) defines the available flags and default values.
findings.problem: 'Choose presentation and budgets' only shows how to keep a partial result in an envelope. An instructor whose long loop trace stops with exit 3 wants a complete ordinary trace. The guide never shows raising one budget (for example --max-snapshots) or --unlimited. The tracer's own stderr recommends both, and no guide or tutorial mentions --unlimited. The numeric defaults needed to choose a new value are also missing. Line 318 sends readers to the CLI reference for 'default values', but for budgets that page only says 'Finite instructor defaults' and the help prints no defaults. The numbers live in BOUNDED_TRACING.md. troubleshooting.md:56 says 'Tune that limit' and links back here, so the loop never answers how.

evidence.detail: Exit 3, 0-byte stdout. Stderr: 'Trace stopped: snapshot_limit. Increase the limit or use --unlimited; use --result-envelope for partial traces.' Without --max-snapshots but with --unlimited: exit 0.
instructorDefaults() = 10_000 ms, 10_000 snapshots, 1 MiB output, ... (the numbers listed in BOUNDED_TRACING.md:8-11).
--unlimited: 'Disable default budgets; explicit limits still apply.'
No matches.
Budgets row: 'Finite instructor defaults.' Numeric defaults are deferred to bounded tracing (cli.md:188-190).

findings.title: Isolation disclaimer covers only reused workers, implying dedicated or fresh guests isolate jobs
findings.quote: Workers can reuse guest JVMs for single-stack jobs. Each job's source, output, observations, and retained snapshots belong to that job; reused workers do not provide OS isolation. Multithread jobs use dedicated guests. For hosted untrusted submissions, follow the [runner contract](../RUNNER_CONTRACT.md), including its one-disposable-tracer-process-per-job requirement.
findings.problem: The "no OS isolation" warning is attached only to reused workers. The next sentence contrasts them with dedicated guests. A reader can conclude that fresh guests (multithread jobs, or `--max-jobs-per-worker 1`) isolate jobs, and that only hosted submissions need extra care. In fact every guest runs as an ordinary JVM under the tracer user's account, with that account's file and network access, and jobs can affect the host and each other. The page leaves out the protocol reference's rule that batch tracing is only for trusted workloads or must run inside external isolation. An instructor or integrator batch-processing untrusted student submissions on a workstation or server, without hosting them, gets no warning. The page also never says plainly that the per-job-process rule means several untrusted submissions must not share one batch-trace stream.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar batch-trace --workers 1 --max-jobs-per-worker 1 -i fileleak.ndjson (scratch dir; job "writer" calls Files.writeString(Path.of("written-by-job.txt"), "job-1"); job "reader" prints Files.readString of the same path; both use "inspection":"FIELDS")
evidence.detail: Output: `writer completed 'wrote\n'` and `reader completed 'job-1\n'`. The file written-by-job.txt appeared in the tracer's working directory. A fresh guest per job with FIELDS inspection still writes to the host filesystem, and a later job reads what it wrote.

Guests are launched through the default JDI LaunchingConnector with only `-Djava.awt.headless=true -classpath ...` (plus optional loader and preview flags). No sandbox or OS restriction is applied, whether the guest is reused or dedicated.
For a multithread job, prepareGuest closes the persistent session and dispatch uses TraceDispatch.dedicated(). Dedicated and persistent guests differ in lifecycle, not in isolation.

The protocol reference states the stronger rule: "Class-loader separation does not provide OS isolation. Use batch tracing only for trusted workloads or within suitable external isolation." The tutorial omits it.
"Run one disposable Tracer process per job." A multi-job batch-trace stream cannot meet this for untrusted submissions.

findings.fix: Rewrite the paragraph so the safety statement covers every worker setting. Suggested text: "Every batch job's code runs as an ordinary JVM with your account's file, network, and process access. This applies whether the guest is reused or dedicated (multithread jobs, or `--max-jobs-per-worker 1`). The tracer keeps each job's source, output, input observations, and retained snapshots separate, but jobs can still affect the host and each other through files and other OS resources. Use batch tracing only for trusted programs or inside external isolation. For hosted untrusted submissions, the runner contract requires one disposable tracer process per job, so do not send several untrusted submissions through one batch-trace stream."

findings.title: No how-to shows how to turn existing .java files into NDJSON batch requests
findings.quote: Save this as UTF-8 `jobs.ndjson`. Keep each object on one physical line.
findings.problem: Every batch example in the docs uses Java source typed by hand as a JSON string literal on one line. A reader with real submissions (multi-line files containing quotes, backslashes, or several files) must JSON-escape each file into a one-line `source` string and assign distinct IDs. No page shows how to do this. Pasting a multi-line file as-is splits the record, because input is read one physical line at a time. docs/index.md sends readers who want to "Consume JSON or process jobs" to this tutorial, and the "Use the tracer" sidebar group has no batch how-to. Readers are left to work out the escaping themselves.

findings.original_problem: Every batch example in the docs uses Java source typed by hand as a JSON string literal on one line. A reader with real submissions (multi-line files containing quotes, backslashes, or several files) must JSON-escape each file into a one-line `source` string and assign distinct IDs. No page shows how to do this. Pasting a multi-line file as-is splits the record, because input is read one physical line at a time. docs/index.md sends readers who want to "Consume JSON or process jobs" to this tutorial, and the "Use the tracer" sidebar group has no batch how-to. Readers are left to work out the escaping themselves.

findings.title: Separate unchecked PowerShell pipeline where the --input option works in every shell
findings.quote: **PowerShell** does not support shell input redirection with `<`. For this UTF-8 text example, use PowerShell 7.4+:
findings.problem: The tutorial works around PowerShell's missing `<` with a second, shell-specific `Get-Content` pipeline that check_docs.py never runs. batch-trace already accepts `-i/--input`, which opens the file directly and always decodes it as UTF-8. One command could therefore serve Bash, Command Prompt, and PowerShell, and the page never mentions the option. Readers maintain and follow two commands where one would do, and the untested one re-encodes the input through the shell.

evidence.detail: Output includes: `-i, --input=<input>       Input path to NDJSON file (defaults to stdin if omitted).`
--input opens the file with Files.newInputStream. Input is always decoded with StandardCharsets.UTF_8, whatever the shell.
exit=0; all three responses were written. Reading through --input works the same as stdin.
"`check_docs.py` does not execute native **PowerShell** or **Command Prompt** alternatives", so the separate PowerShell block is unverified.

findings.fix: Replace both commands with one: `java -jar code-tracer.jar batch-trace --input jobs.ndjson --workers 1 --max-in-flight 2 --max-jobs-per-worker 100 > results.ndjson`. Say it works in Bash, Command Prompt, and PowerShell 7.4+, keeping the existing 7.4+ requirement for the output redirection. Keep it inside the batch-command markers so check_docs.py executes it. Add a short note that the batch protocol reference also accepts NDJSON on standard input.

findings.title: Says API Guardian is 'needed' to compile; javac succeeds without it, with warnings
findings.quote: API Guardian is also needed on a manual compile classpath.
findings.problem: Compiling against the regular library JAR without API Guardian succeeds; javac only warns about the missing annotation enum. The linked reference says API Guardian is included 'to avoid missing annotation warnings'. The tutorial's 'needed' overstates this and disagrees with the reference it links to. It is harmless in practice but can drift. The neighboring claim that the regular JAR alone is insufficient at runtime is accurate.

evidence.ref: javac -cp cs1302-tracer-4.2.0-SNAPSHOT.jar TraceExample.java (scratch dir, tutorial source); then java -cp "cs1302-tracer-4.2.0-SNAPSHOT.jar:." TraceExample
evidence.detail: javac exit 0 with '3 warnings': 'warning: unknown enum constant Status.STABLE / reason: class file for org.apiguardian.api.API$Status not found'. The run then fails with NoClassDefFoundError: com/google/gson/GsonBuilder, which confirms lines 89-90.
'when compiling against the regular JAR by hand, also include the API Guardian JAR on the compile classpath to avoid missing annotation warnings.'
apiguardian-api 1.1.2 is a compile-scope dependency, so Maven consumers receive it transitively.

findings.fix: Reword: 'When compiling against the regular JAR by hand, also add the API Guardian JAR to the compile classpath to avoid missing-annotation warnings (builds using -Werror fail without it).'

findings.title: Exit-3 row says to tune a budget, but some exit-3 stops are fixed checks no option or --unlimited lifts
findings.quote: | Exit code `3` and no JSON from ordinary tracing | Read the budget diagnostic. Tune that limit for your trusted example, or follow [the partial-result recipe](tracing.md#keep-partial-results-when-a-budget-stops-tracing). | Ordinary budget exhaustion writes no trace JSON. Redirected output can therefore be an empty file. |
findings.problem: The row treats every ordinary exit 3 as a budget that can be tuned. Any stop reason that is not an error is classified as "stopped" and exits 3. That includes fixed checks with no matching option: unsupported_virtual_thread, value_nesting_limit, inline_value_cycle, and type_nesting_limit. A reader whose --multithread trace of a virtual-thread program exits 3 follows this row, raises limits or adds --unlimited, and gets the same stop. The row also gives no way to map a stop code such as trace_limit or element_limit to the option that controls it.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i V.java --multithread -f modern --unlimited > v2.json  (V.java starts one Thread.ofVirtual() thread)
evidence.detail: stderr: "Trace stopped: unsupported_virtual_thread. Increase the limit or use --unlimited; use --result-envelope for partial traces." exit=3, output size 0. The same command without --unlimited gives the same stop. Without --multithread (-a only) the program traces with exit 0.
status is "failed" only for reasons ending in "error", guest_exception, or guest_exit. Every other stop reason is "stopped".
An ordinary "stopped" result prints "Trace stopped: <reason>. Increase the limit or use --unlimited" and exits 3.
Fixed stop reasons that come from no TraceLimits option.
"Unlimited resource budgets do not disable fixed representation safety checks". Lists unsupported_virtual_thread and the nesting stops.

findings.fix: Rewrite the row: exit 3 is a controlled stop, so read the stop code in the diagnostic. For resource codes (timeout, snapshot_limit, output_limit, heap_limit, element_limit, trace_limit, source_limit, source_file_limit, thread_limit, frame_limit, snapshot_byte_limit), raise the matching option. Add a short code-to-option mapping, or link to a mapping in BOUNDED_TRACING#limits. For unsupported_virtual_thread, value_nesting_limit, inline_value_cycle, and type_nesting_limit, say that no budget or --unlimited removes them: change the program or capture mode (for example, omit --multithread for virtual threads) and link to BOUNDED_TRACING.md#representation-nesting.

findings.title: Repeated-output row calls every snapshot a cumulative prefix; selected-breakpoint hits show final output
findings.quote: | Output appears repeatedly in snapshots | Read each snapshot as a cumulative prefix; do not concatenate every `stdout` value. | The final snapshot can receive trailing guest output. See the [trace model](../explanation/trace-model.md). |
findings.problem: With ordinary selected-breakpoint output (--breakpoints), each retained hit carries the program's final stdout and stderr, including text printed after that stop. That is exactly where the same output repeats across entries. Following this row, a reader would treat the stdout at a stop as the output printed so far. For example, they would conclude that a println had already run at a stop that comes before it. The interpretation column limits the effect to "the final snapshot". The linked trace-model page says the opposite: read output according to the selected mode.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Err.java -b 3,4 -f modern > sel.json  (line 3: System.out.println("out"); line 4: System.err.println("err"))

findings.title: Running-JDK mismatch row links back to the checkpoint that sent the reader here
findings.quote: | Direct JAR execution reports a different running JDK | Follow the [installation checkpoint](installation.md#verify-your-installation), which compares explicit-path and bare `java` invocation. | Changing the `java.home` property cannot switch the JVM that is already running. |
findings.problem: When the installation checkpoint fails, it sends the reader to this page's startup section. This row sends the reader back to that same checkpoint, so it gives no corrective step. The interpretation mentions the `java.home` property instead of the actual cause: JAVA_HOME (or PATH) selects one JDK, but the `java` command the reader typed started another. The concrete fixes appear only in the raw diagnostic and the CLI reference.

evidence.detail: "If either fails, preserve its stderr diagnostic and follow [startup troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#the-tracer-does-not-start). A failure mentioning a different running JDK means the direct invocation and environment selection still disagree."

exit=1: "The running JDK .../openjdk@25/... differs from the selected JDK .../openjdk@21/.... Launch with .../openjdk@21/.../bin/java -jar code-tracer.jar. Set JAVA_HOME to a full stable JDK 21 or later, or unset it and put that JDK's bin directory first on PATH."
Compares the selected JDK's java.home against the running JVM's java.home and emits the diagnostic above.

findings.fix: Give a direct action: run the selected JDK's executable ("$JAVA_HOME/bin/java" -jar code-tracer.jar), or make bare `java` match. To make it match, re-run [select an installed JDK](installation.md#select-an-installed-jdk-for-this-terminal-session), which puts $JAVA_HOME/bin first on PATH, then use the alias/shim row if the mismatch persists. Alternatively, unset JAVA_HOME so the tracer uses PATH. Replace the interpretation with: JAVA_HOME (or PATH) chose one JDK, but the `java` you typed started another. The tracer checks against the selection and cannot switch the running JVM.

findings.title: Says diagnostics always go to tracer stderr, but --result-envelope puts them in stdout JSON
findings.quote: The tracer's own diagnostics are separate: they go to the tracer process's stderr, outside the JSON trace. Redirecting its stdout saves the JSON result while leaving those diagnostics visible in the terminal.
findings.problem: This is only true of ordinary output, but the page states it without qualification. With --result-envelope, job diagnostics such as compile errors and guest exception types go into the envelope's `diagnostics` array on stdout, and the tracer's stderr stays empty. Redirecting stdout therefore hides them instead of leaving them visible. Six lines later the page says envelopes 'report completion and diagnostics', so an integrator automating envelope runs can reasonably conclude that diagnostics appear in both places, and read or monitor stderr expecting them. Only option-validation errors still reach stderr in envelope mode.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Bad.java --result-envelope --format modern > env.json 2>env.err   (Bad.java contains `int x = ;`)
evidence.detail: Exit 1. env.err is 0 bytes. env.json has status "failed", stopReason "compile_error", trace null, and diagnostics ["java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Parsing failed with the following errors: [(..."].

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Boom.java --result-envelope --format modern > envb.json 2>envb.err   (Boom.java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on line 5)
evidence.detail: Exit 1. envb.err is 0 bytes. The envelope has stopReason "guest_exception" and diagnostics ["java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException"].

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Bad.java --format modern > bad.json 2> bad.err
evidence.detail: Ordinary mode for contrast: exit 1, bad.json is 0 bytes, and bad.err starts with "Unable to generate trace! Parsing failed ...". The page's statement holds only for this mode.

The envelope path returns through runBounded, which prints the TraceResult, including diagnostics, with System.out.println (line 430). Only the ordinary path prints "Unable to generate trace!" or "Trace stopped:" to System.err (lines 361-363).
Exit 2, stdout empty, stderr "Trace limits must be nonnegative; 0 is unlimited" (App.java:346-348). Validation errors are the only output that reaches stderr in envelope mode.

findings.title: CLI source discovery from the -i path and the stdin working directory is undocumented
findings.quote: Source discovery keeps its existing caller-specific policy.
findings.problem: Under TRUSTED inspection, trace (ordinary and envelope) and list-breakpoints compile extra host sources as well as the submitted text. For a packaged program, the source root is inferred from the package-matching ancestors of the -i path. For stdin input, it comes from the tracer's working directory, trying ./<pkg>, src/main/java/<pkg>, and src/<pkg>. Default-package programs get no neighbour discovery. FIELDS and --multithread turn discovery off. The CLI reference documents none of this: the Source row says only that source is read from stdin, and line 321 points to an undefined 'existing caller-specific policy'. In practice, a stdin trace can silently depend on the runner's working directory, and discovered files are compiled without appearing in `sources`. An instructor who expects a default-package helper next to Main.java to be compiled gets a compile error. batch.md documents the batch equivalent; the CLI has no equivalent text.

evidence.detail: findSourceRoot returns empty when there is no package declaration. With an input path it walks package-matching parents. Without one (stdin) it tries the candidates ".", "src/main/java", "src" relative to the process working directory.
FIELDS (including FIELDS implied by --multithread) selects SUBMITTED_ONLY. The ordinary CLI selects NEIGHBORS_OR_COMPILED and the envelope selects NEIGHBORS.

evidence.ref: (cd p && java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -f modern < UseHPkg.txt)   where p/demo/H.java exists and the stdin source is 'package demo; class UseH' calling H.v()
evidence.detail: exit=0, steps[-1].stdout "7\n", sources keys ["demo/UseH.java"] (H.java was compiled but is not listed). Adding --result-envelope gives status completed. Adding --result-envelope --inspection FIELDS gives failed/compile_error. Running from a different cwd gives exit=1.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -f modern -i n/UseH.java   (default package; sibling n/H.java defines H)
evidence.detail: exit=1: 'Unable to generate trace! Compilation of provided Java source code failed ... error: cannot find symbol ... variable H'
Batch documents its rule: 'packaged batch sources can also discover matching source roots in the process working directory, `src/main/java`, or `src`.' The CLI reference has no counterpart.

findings.title: Default final-state capture fails with an internal error when main ends with System.exit
findings.quote: | Capture | Final main-exit state. | `--all-breakpoints` (`-a`) for chronological capture, or `--breakpoints` (`-b`) for selected locations. |
findings.problem: An ordinary trace with no -a or -b only works if main returns. If the program calls System.exit (even System.exit(0)), the command exits 1 with an internal NullPointerException message. The page gives no precondition and no workaround. The same program traces fine with -a or -b, and the envelope default returns completed with an empty steps array. Instructors tracing menu-loop programs that end with System.exit(0) are blocked and get no actionable diagnostic. The root cause is in the implementation; the docs should at least state the limitation.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Exit0.java   (main: int x = 1; System.exit(0);)
evidence.detail: exit=1, stdout empty, stderr: 'Unable to generate trace! Cannot invoke "java.util.List.getLast()" because the return value of "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null'. The result is the same with -f modern.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -a -f modern -i Exit0.java ; java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -b 4 -i Exit0.java
evidence.detail: Both exit 0. The -a run produces 2 steps at lines [3,4]. With --result-envelope and no -a/-b, the result is {"status":"completed","stopReason":null} with 0 steps.
The final-state path calls selected(prepared, List.of(), stdin, true).get(-1).getLast(). There is no main-exit entry when the guest exits through System.exit.

findings.fix: Document the observed default-capture failure and available capture-mode workaround in the manual CLI reference. A Java implementation correction is a separate task requiring authorization.

findings.title: Selected-breakpoint values become arrays when two files share a line number
findings.quote: | `--breakpoints 4` | A root object with `breakpoints`; `breakpoints["4"]` is the latest snapshot at that location. | A root dictionary; `["4"]` is a complete Python Tutor payload whose `trace` contains the latest snapshot. |
findings.problem: Selected-breakpoint keys are bare line numbers, not locations. In a multi-file submission, selecting the same line number in two files puts both hits under one key. In latest mode that key's value then becomes an array of snapshots (modern) or an array of payloads (Python Tutor), one per file, instead of the single snapshot or payload the table promises. An integrator coding to the table crashes or misreads the result, and the key alone does not say which file a hit belongs to. The CLI help advertises file-qualified selections such as '12,Helper.java:5'.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace --format modern -b 'demo/Main.java:4,demo/Helper.java:4' < bundle.txt   (two-file bundle: src/demo/Helper.java and src/demo/Main.java, line 4 executable in both)
evidence.detail: breakpoints => {'4': ('list', ['demo/Main.java', 'demo/Helper.java'])}. The same command without --format modern gives {'4': ('list', ['demo/Main.java', 'demo/Helper.java'])}, i.e. an array of two Python Tutor payloads. No --accumulate-breakpoints was given.
keepLatestOnly keys by Integer line and keeps one latest snapshot per source file under that key.
Modern and Python Tutor latest rendering emit a single value when list.size() == 1 and a JSON array otherwise.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -f modern -b demo/Helper.java:5,demo/Main.java:5 < bundle.txt (two-file bundle in the tracing-guide delimiter format; line 5 executes in both files)
evidence.detail: breakpoints has a single key '5' whose value is a list of 2: [('demo/Main.java', 5, 'step_line'), ('demo/Helper.java', 5, 'step_line')]. No --accumulate-breakpoints was given.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -f pytutor -b demo/Helper.java:5,demo/Main.java:5 < bundle.txt
evidence.detail: Root key '5' is a list of 2 complete Python Tutor payloads, one with trace[].file 'demo/Main.java' and one with 'demo/Helper.java'.

evidence.ref: java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -f modern --result-envelope -b demo/Helper.java:5,demo/Main.java:5 < bundle.txt
evidence.detail: completed; steps [('demo/Main.java', 5), ('demo/Helper.java', 5)]. The envelope sequence keeps both hits in capture order without the grouping ambiguity.

keepLatestOnly keeps 'the latest snapshot per source file for each line' in a Map<Integer, List<ExecutionSnapshot>>. storeBreakpoint keys by int line and replaces only entries with the same sourcePath.
Non-accumulated rendering writes a single snapshot when list.size() == 1 and writes the whole list otherwise, for both modern and Python Tutor.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace --breakpoints 4 --format modern < submission.txt (the guide's two-file bundle)
evidence.detail: breakpoints keys ['4']. Value is a list of 2 snapshots with file demo/Main.java and demo/Helper.java. Exit 0.
Root {'4': [2 Python Tutor payloads]}. The modern format likewise gives breakpoints['4'] as a list of 2.

Non-accumulated rendering puts a single snapshot when the per-line list has size 1, otherwise the whole list (same pattern for pytutor at 177-184). Snapshots are stored by int line (DebugTraceHelper.java:332, 1147-1149).
'`--breakpoints 4` | A root object with `breakpoints`; `breakpoints["4"]` is the latest snapshot at that location.'

findings.fix: In the table and its notes, state that keys are unqualified line numbers. When a selection includes the same line number in more than one file, latest mode yields an array with one latest snapshot or payload per file; consumers tell them apart by `file`. Accumulated arrays interleave the files in hit order. Tell consumers to accept object-or-array values, or to use --all-breakpoints or --result-envelope for a uniform sequence. Changing to file-qualified keys would be a separate format decision.

findings.original_problem: Selected-breakpoint keys are bare line numbers, not locations. In a multi-file submission, selecting the same line number in two files puts both hits under one key. In latest mode that key's value then becomes an array of snapshots (modern) or an array of payloads (Python Tutor), one per file, instead of the single snapshot or payload the table promises. An integrator coding to the table crashes or misreads the result, and the key alone does not say which file a hit belongs to. The CLI help advertises file-qualified selections such as '12,Helper.java:5'.
findings.original_fix: In the table and its notes, state that keys are unqualified line numbers. When a selection includes the same line number in more than one file, latest mode yields an array with one latest snapshot or payload per file; consumers tell them apart by `file`. Accumulated arrays interleave the files in hit order. Tell consumers to accept object-or-array values, or to use --all-breakpoints or --result-envelope for a uniform sequence. Changing to file-qualified keys would be a separate format decision.

findings.title: Envelope, batch, and Java modern payloads carry explicit null properties the page never mentions
findings.quote: Modern selected output can contain a `breakpoints` mapping. Envelope mode always carries a format-specific sequence root when a trace is available.
findings.problem: In envelope mode (CLI --result-envelope, batch responses, and Java TraceOutcome JSON), the modern payload is serialized with explicit nulls. The payload root contains `"breakpoints": null`. Every step contains `"threads": null` and `"triggeringThreadId": null`. Static frames contain `"this": null`. Heap objects contain `fields`/`elements`/`value`/`sam` set to null. Ordinary CLI output omits all of these. The page documents shapes only from ordinary output, and line 691 suggests that the presence of `breakpoints` signals selected output. An integrator who reuses one parser for ordinary and envelope payloads and detects shape by key presence (for example `'breakpoints' in payload` or `'threads' in step`) takes the wrong branch and fails on null. A strict schema built from the documented modern example rejects every envelope or batch payload. BOUNDED_TRACING.md:115 calls the envelope `trace` 'a normal format-specific root', and output.md:150 says 'Without `--multithread`, the existing output shape is preserved', so readers have no warning.

findings.original_problem: In envelope mode (CLI --result-envelope, batch responses, and Java TraceOutcome JSON), the modern payload is serialized with explicit nulls. findings.title: Unrecognized inspection values such as "fields" silently run TRUSTED inspection
findings.quote: | `inspection` | `TRUSTED` (default) or `FIELDS`. |
findings.problem: The rows next to `inspection` accept lowercase values case-insensitively (`pytutor`, `modern`, `fqn`, `simple`). findings.title: The page never fully says which failures lose the id or how to correlate null-id responses
findings.quote:
A structurally parsed request with invalid format or type-style settings uses `validation_error` and
retains its `id`.
findings.problem: The page tells clients to use `id` to correlate responses. It lists the null-id cases as nesting depth, malformed JSON, literal null, and (in the dependency section only) wrong JSON types in classPath. Many more requests that bind incorrectly also return `parse_error` with a null id. These include a negative, fractional, or too-large limit, `"allBreakpoints": 1`, and `"breakpoints": "4"`. A reader would expect a semantically invalid limit to keep its id, the way format, type-style, and classPath-shape errors do. The page also never says that submission order yields exactly one response per nonblank record in input order. That is the only way to match a null-id failure to its request. Nor does it warn that with `--completion-order` such failures cannot be correlated at all. A client that waits for a response for every id it sent can wait forever or misattribute the failure.

evidence.detail: Any exception from JsonNesting.validate or gson.fromJson returns BatchJobResponse(null, ...) with stopReason parse_error. The id is lost even when the JSON is syntactically valid.
Negative budgets or a timeout above Long.MAX_VALUE/1_000_000 throw while Gson constructs the record, so they surface as parse failures.
Each nonblank record is submitted once. In submission order, writes are chained with previous.thenCombine, so responses follow input order.
Each response: id None, format 'unknown', status 'failed', stopReason 'parse_error', phase 'parse'. Contrast {"id":"fmt-bad","format":"xml"}: id 'fmt-bad', validation_error.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar batch-trace -i misc.ndjson (second line is `{not json`)
evidence.detail: The malformed record's response: id=None, status=failed, complete=False, stopReason=parse_error, phase=parse, format=unknown. It cannot be correlated by ID.
Nesting-limit, malformed, and literal-null requests all produce `new BatchJobResponse(null, ...)`.

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar batch-trace --workers 1 --max-in-flight 2 --max-jobs-per-worker 100 < jobs.ndjson > results.ndjson (tutorial input)
evidence.detail: The `hello` result has diagnostics ["FIELDS inspection uses raw fields for collections and wrappers; guest methods and stream flush are not invoked."]. Both results also contain stopReason, phase, counters, limits, and trace, none of which the page mentions or links to.
The request-field table, the null-id parse-failure rule, and the envelope field definitions all exist, but the tutorial links to none of them for these purposes.

findings.fix: Replace the format/type-style sentence with a general rule. A record whose JSON cannot be bound to the request types (any field with the wrong JSON type, or a non-integer, negative, or out-of-range limit) gets `parse_error` with a null id. Checks made after binding (format, typeStyle, multithread with pytutor, classPath shapes and glob syntax) return `validation_error` and keep the id. Add that in the default submission order, every nonblank record yields exactly one response in input order (unless an oversized record aborts the stream), so null-id responses can be matched by position. With `--completion-order` they cannot be matched, so clients should validate requests before submitting or use submission order.

Nor does it warn that with `--completion-order` such failures cannot be correlated at all. A client that waits for a response for every id it sent can wait forever or misattribute the failure.
findings.original_fix: Replace the format/type-style sentence with a general rule. A record whose JSON cannot be bound to the request types (any field with the wrong JSON type, or a non-integer, negative, or out-of-range limit) gets `parse_error` with a null id. Checks made after binding (format, typeStyle, multithread with pytutor, classPath shapes and glob syntax) return `validation_error` and keep the id. Add that in the default submission order, every nonblank record yields exactly one response in input order (unless an oversized record aborts the stream), so null-id responses can be matched by position. With `--completion-order` they cannot be matched, so clients should validate requests before submitting or use submission order.

It never says that BatchTracer reuses guest JVMs across jobs, which makes it unsuitable for hosted untrusted submissions. The runner contract requires one disposable tracer process per job, and the batch reference says to use batch tracing only for trusted workloads. findings.title: snapshot_byte_limit is described as a thread-capture stop reason but also stops single-stack jobs
findings.problem: The page says thread capture adds snapshot_byte_limit and lists the snapshotBytes batch field with the thread fields. In the code, --max-snapshot-bytes / snapshotBytes applies to every capture mode. The ordinary 8 MiB default (line 11) therefore applies to every single-stack CLI and Java API job. snapshot_byte_limit is also missing from the stop-code table (137-149), so this sentence is the page's only listing of it. An integrator would reasonably decide that single-stack jobs never stop with snapshot_byte_limit and leave that code unhandled.

evidence.detail: allocate() calls enforce(buildingBytes, limits.snapshotBytes(), "snapshot_byte_limit") for every snapshot. It is not gated on threadCapture.
commit() calls enforce(size, limits.snapshotBytes(), "snapshot_byte_limit") for every admitted snapshot.

Single-stack job (no --multithread): exit=3, status 'stopped', stopReason 'snapshot_byte_limit', droppedSnapshots 1. The same run without the envelope prints 'Trace stopped: snapshot_byte_limit.' and exits 3.

findings.title: Null vs empty trace rule is caller-dependent, and the page says 'failed' where stopped jobs also apply
findings.quote:
An empty sequence means capture ran without a completed snapshot. Null means
no usable trace payload was available, for example after compilation failure,
serializer failure, or a failed Java/batch capture that completed no snapshots.
findings.problem: The page states the empty-vs-null rule as general and gives 'failed Java/batch capture' as the only Java/batch null case. 'failed' is a literal status value on this page (line 109). In fact, Java and batch results return null for any non-completed job (stopped or failed) that committed no snapshot, even when a guest ran. The CLI envelope returns an empty sequence for the same stop. So the same stop on the same program gives `[]` from `trace --result-envelope` and `null` from batch-trace. An integrator who uses null vs [] to tell 'capture ran' from 'capture unavailable' will misclassify batch and Java stops, or index into a null trace after a stopped batch job.

evidence.detail: workerRecovery (Java/batch) returns null whenever !session.traceAvailable() || session.snapshots().isEmpty(), whatever the stop reason.
CLI envelope path uses session.snapshots() (possibly empty) whenever a guest was attached, so it renders an empty sequence.
batch: 's stopped snapshot_byte_limit trace=None' (guestExitCode 137, droppedSnapshots 1). CLI: 'cli stopped snapshot_byte_limit 0' (trace.trace == []).

findings.fix: Make the rule caller-specific. CLI envelopes: null when no guest was launched (source, compile or serializer failure), an empty sequence when a guest ran but committed no snapshot. Java and batch results: null whenever a stopped or failed job committed no snapshot, and an empty sequence only for a completed job with no retained snapshot. Tell consumers to check status and counters.snapshotsCaptured instead of inferring capture from null vs [].

Integrators reading counters must guess or reverse-engineer snapshotsCaptured, snapshotsRetained, retainedBytes, droppedSnapshots, elapsedMillis, stdoutBytes, stderrBytes and guestExitCode. findings.title: Item 3 names 'tracer and compiler' but omits the guest JVM, which keeps running after Tracer is killed
findings.quote: entire job and its descendants, including the tracer and compiler.
findings.problem: The page never says that the untrusted program runs in a separate guest JVM launched through JDI. Item 3 names the tracer and the compiler as the job's processes, but javac runs inside the Tracer JVM. The actual descendants are the guest JVM (dedicated or reusable) and the CLI's java/javac version probes. findings.title: Finite limits are only 'preferred', but the recommended --result-envelope makes every omitted limit unlimited
findings.quote: Prefer `--result-envelope`, `FIELDS`, and explicit finite values for all limits described in [bounded tracing](BOUNDED_TRACING.md).
findings.problem: The contract recommends envelope mode but treats finite limits as optional ('Prefer'). It does not warn that --result-envelope switches every omitted limit to 0 (unlimited); the finite instructor defaults apply only to ordinary tracing. A runner that adopts the envelope and sets only some limits (for example --timeout-ms) gets unlimited snapshots, output, heap objects, trace bytes, and source size. BOUNDED_TRACING states this as a requirement ('Supply finite budgets for every hosted job'), so the two pages disagree on whether it is mandatory.

evidence.detail: Envelope limits: {'timeoutMillis': 0, 'snapshots': 0, 'outputBytes': 0, 'heapObjects': 0, 'elements': 0, 'traceBytes': 0, 'sourceBytes': 0, 'sourceFiles': 0, 'threads': 0, 'frames': 0, 'snapshotBytes': 0}
Only timeoutMillis becomes 5000; every other limit stays 0 (unlimited).
'Supply finite budgets for every hosted job. In envelope mode, omitted budget options use zero (unlimited).' This is a requirement there and only a preference in the runner contract.

findings.fix: Use mandatory finite-budget wording and a short omitted-means-unlimited reminder, with a direct limits link; avoid duplicating the entire CLI option catalog.

findings.title: 'Minimal environment' omits Tracer's JDK and JAVA_HOME/PATH preconditions; a cleared env fails every job
findings.quote: A nonprivileged execution identity, a minimal environment without secrets, and access only to required runtime files, submitted sources, and approved binary dependencies.
findings.problem: The page never says what runtime the containment unit must contain or which environment variables Tracer needs. The CLI requires a full stable JDK 21+ (javac and JDI, not a JRE). Before doing any work, its preflight requires either JAVA_HOME pointing to that JDK or PATH containing its java and javac, and the running JVM must be that JDK. A runner that follows 'minimal environment' literally (for example env -i or a sandbox --clearenv) gets exit 1 with empty stdout and no envelope for every job.

evidence.detail: exit=1, stdout 0 bytes, stderr: 'code-tracer: JDK environment check failed: No executable java was found on PATH. The preflight runs java/javac version probes as child processes.
Compilation requires ToolProvider.getSystemJavaCompiler(), which needs a full JDK.
The JDK environment preflight rules (JAVA_HOME authoritative, PATH fallback, matching versions, exit 1) are documented here, but the runner contract does not link to them.

findings.title: 'Necessary intra-job JDI transport' is never specified (loopback TCP on an ephemeral port)
findings.quote: Permit necessary intra-job JDI transport without exposing debugger endpoints outside the containment unit.
findings.problem: Item 5 tells the runner to allow the JDI transport while restricting networking, but no user-facing page says what that transport is. On Linux, each guest launch has the Tracer listen on 127.0.0.1 at an ephemeral TCP port, and the guest connects to localhost:<port>. A runner cannot write the network policy without knowing this. A namespace with loopback down, or a policy that blocks loopback TCP, breaks every launch. In a direct backend where jobs share a network namespace, any local process can connect to the listener during launch.

evidence.detail: Uses Bootstrap.virtualMachineManager().defaultConnector() (CommandLineLaunch) with default transport settings.
Without shared memory (Windows-only), the launcher calls transportService().startListening(). An empty host maps to InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress().

evidence.ref: lsof -nP -a -p <tracer pid> -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN (polled during java -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace -i Main.java)
ps -ax -o pid,ppid,command | grep jdwp (during a trace)
evidence.detail: Guest command line: '... -Xrunjdwp:transport=dt_socket,address=localhost:52595,suspend=y,includevirtualthreads=n Main'
The only hit is RUNNER_CONTRACT.md:20 ('container-management sockets'). No user page describes the JDI transport.

findings.fix: Expand item 5: 'JDI uses a loopback TCP connection: while launching each guest, Tracer listens on 127.0.0.1 at an ephemeral port and the guest JVM connects to localhost:<port>. The job's network namespace must have loopback up and localhost resolving to 127.0.0.1. Give each job its own network namespace, because any process sharing loopback can connect to the listener during launch.'

findings.title: Contract omits that Tracer prepares sources in java.io.tmpdir, which survives a kill
findings.quote: A private, disposable workspace with no concurrent writers during source preparation.
findings.problem: Items 1 and 6 require a private workspace during source preparation and cleanup after termination, but the page never says where Tracer writes. Source preparation writes the submitted sources and compiled classes into a new code-tracer* directory under the Tracer JVM's java.io.tmpdir, not the working directory. --copy-class-path copies go to tracer-class-path-* there as well. The guest JVM runs in the Tracer's working directory but uses the default java.io.tmpdir even when Tracer's is overridden. After a forced kill these directories remain. A direct-backend runner that treats the working directory as 'the workspace' will leave a shared temp directory exposed during preparation and will leave residue behind after timeouts.

evidence.detail: Files.createTempDirectory("code-tracer") holds the written sources and javac output.
With copying enabled: Files.createTempDirectory("tracer-class-path-").

evidence.ref: cd $D/work; TMPDIR=$D/work java -Djava.io.tmpdir=$D/tmp -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace --result-envelope -i Main.java & (Main sleeps 30 s); find $D/tmp; kill -9 <tracer>; find $D/tmp
evidence.detail: During the run: D/tmp/code-tracer7571436768378997599/{Main.java,Main.class}. After kill -9 the directory and both files remain.

evidence.ref: java -Djava.io.tmpdir=$D/tmp -jar target/code-tracer.jar trace --result-envelope -i Main.java (guest prints java.io.tmpdir and user.dir)
evidence.detail: Guest stdout: '/var/folders/y6/.../T/' (system default, not $D/tmp) and the tracer's working directory.

findings.fix: Document containment and cleanup of both host-tracer and guest temporary files. A tracer -Djava.io.tmpdir setting relocates tracer-owned directories only and is not forwarded to the guest. Use a private per-job filesystem/temp namespace (for example a private /tmp mount on Linux) to contain guest temporary files as well.

findings.original_problem: Items 1 and 6 require a private workspace during source preparation and cleanup after termination, but the page never says where Tracer writes. Source preparation writes the submitted sources and compiled classes into a new code-tracer* directory under the Tracer JVM's java.io.tmpdir, not the working directory. --copy-class-path copies go to tracer-class-path-* there as well. findings.title: Job interface covers the CLI only; Java API callers sent here are not told their own JVM must be per-job
findings.quote: Run one disposable Tracer process per job.
findings.problem: java-api.md sends hosted embedders to this contract, but the job interface is written only in CLI terms (CLI flags, --result-envelope, FIELDS, stdout). Tracer.trace parses and compiles the submission inside the calling JVM and launches the guest from it. Under this contract, therefore, the embedding JVM itself must be the disposable per-job process inside the containment unit, not a long-lived server. The page never says this. It also never gives the API equivalents: InspectionPolicy.FIELDS (the TraceRequest default is TRUSTED), explicit finite TraceLimits (the default is instructorDefaults), and outcome.json() as the untrusted result artifact.

findings.title: Migration omits that Tracer.trace returns failures/stops as status with finite default budgets
findings.quote: | `DebugTraceHelper` and JDI-based extraction helpers | `Tracer.trace(TraceRequest)` for self-contained jobs. |
findings.problem: In 3.x, compile failures and budget stops were thrown as exceptions (CompilationHelper.compile threw IllegalArgumentException; TraceSession.Stopped is a RuntimeException), and DebugTraceHelper calls made outside a TraceSession had no budgets. The page tells readers to swap DebugTraceHelper for Tracer.trace(TraceRequest) and getGson() for traceJson(), and lines 4-6 say defaults 'remain unchanged'. It never says that Tracer.trace does not throw for these cases. Instead it returns status/stopReason, and the convenience request applies finite instructor limits (10 s, 1 MiB output, and others). Migrated code that still relies on exceptions and reads only traceJson() gets a well-formed Python Tutor payload with an empty trace for an output-heavy program that traced fully in 3.x, and the literal null for a compile error, with no exception. The integration silently produces wrong results.

evidence.detail: The convenience constructor TraceRequest(String source) passes TraceLimits.instructorDefaults().
instructorDefaults() = 10_000 ms timeout, 10_000 snapshots, 1_048_576 output bytes, and so on.

evidence.ref: git show v3.2.5:src/main/java/cs1302/tracer/trace/DebugTraceHelper.java (lines 371-376); git show v3.2.5:src/main/java/cs1302/tracer/CompilationHelper.java (lines 286-289); git show v3.2.5:src/main/java/cs1302/tracer/execution/TraceSession.java (line 666)
evidence.detail: 3.x helpers ran under TraceLimits.unlimited() when no session was bound. compile() is documented '@throws IllegalArgumentException If the Java program failed to compile'. Stops were 'public static final class Stopped extends RuntimeException'.

evidence.ref: java -cp target/code-tracer.jar Probe2.java big/Main.java (scratch dir; Main prints 2048 lines of 1023 chars; Probe2 calls Tracer.trace(new TraceRequest(src)))
evidence.detail: status=stopped stopReason=output_limit complete=false; traceJson() parses to keys [code, entryFile, sources, stdin, trace, userlog] with 0 trace steps; with .limits(TraceLimits.unlimited()) status=completed.

evidence.ref: java -cp target/code-tracer.jar Probe4.java (Tracer.trace on source 'int x = ;')
evidence.detail: No exception thrown: status=failed phase=compile traceJson=null diag=1.
The reference states the convenience request uses 'finite instructor limits' and that failures 'become outcomes'. The migration page neither states this nor links to it.

findings.fix: Add a 'Behavior changes' section next to the table. Say that Tracer.trace does not throw for compilation failures, guest failures, or budget stops. Callers must check status(), complete(), and stopReason() before using traceJson(), which can be the JSON literal null or a payload with a partial or empty trace. Say that new TraceRequest(source) and TraceRequest.builder(source) apply TraceLimits.instructorDefaults(), whereas 3.x helper calls outside a TraceSession were unbudgeted. For trusted inputs that need the old behavior, use .limits(TraceLimits.unlimited()). Narrow lines 4-6 so they refer to CLI, envelope, and NDJSON defaults only, and note that the one-shot Java caller profile has its own defaults. Link java-api.md#trace-a-submitted-program and BOUNDED_TRACING.md.

findings.title: getGson() row offers json()/writeJson (envelope) as equal to traceJson() (3.x payload)
findings.quote: | `PyTutorSerializer.getGson()` or `ModernTraceSerializer.getGson()` | `TraceOutcome.json()`, `traceJson()`, or `writeJson(Writer)`. |
findings.problem: In 3.x, getGson().toJson(trace) produced the bare trace payload, for example a Python Tutor object with code and trace. The row presents three interchangeable replacements, but json() and writeJson(Writer) return the result envelope (schemaVersion, status, limits, counters, stdout, trace, ...). Only traceJson() returns the payload 3.x produced. A reader who picks json() or writeJson, the first and the Writer-based options, sends an envelope to Python Tutor or to a payload parser and gets the wrong document shape.

findings.fix: Split the replacement. Use traceJson() for the payload that getGson().toJson(trace) used to produce. findings.title: Page omits that Tracer.trace drops 3.x breakpoint-keyed map results for selected breakpoints
findings.quote: | `DebugTraceHelper` and JDI-based extraction helpers | `Tracer.trace(TraceRequest)` for self-contained jobs. |
findings.problem: The 3.x DebugTraceHelper breakpoint methods returned Map<Integer, List<ExecutionSnapshot>> keyed by line, and integrators serialized that map, as the 3.x CLI did. In 4.x, Tracer.trace with selected breakpoints returns a single payload in the batch/envelope convention. The reference says it 'does not reproduce ordinary CLI selected-breakpoint map presentation', and nothing on the migration page warns about this. findings.title: Table leaves out documented 3.x entry points: TraceSession, cancel(), PersistentGuestSession, 2-arg BatchTraceService
findings.quote: | `BatchTraceService` | `BatchTracer` with the same stream protocol. |
findings.problem: The 3.2.5 user docs told library callers to bind a public TraceSession to apply limits and call cancel() from another thread, and to call TraceSession.enableMultithread() for thread capture. 3.x also exposed public PersistentGuestSession (reusable guests), TraceResult (the envelope record), and BatchTraceService(int, int), which defaulted maxInFlight to max(16, 2*workers). None of these has a row. In 4.x, explicit cancellation has no supported replacement, multithread becomes a TraceRequest component, reusable guests exist only through BatchTracer, and BatchTracer has no two-argument form: its builder requires maxInFlight. A reader with TraceSession-based or two-argument BatchTraceService code cannot complete the migration from this page or keep the old admission behavior.

evidence.ref: git show v3.2.5:docs/BOUNDED_TRACING.md (lines 132-135); git show v3.2.5:docs/reference/output.md (lines 117-119)

Only a 4-argument constructor (workers, maxJobsPerWorker, maxInFlight, completionOrder); java-api.md:513-515 says missing builder settings cause IllegalStateException.
'The supported interface does not expose a session handle or an explicit cancellation method.'

findings.fix: Add rows. TraceSession limits, inspection, accumulate, and enableMultithread() map to the TraceRequest limits, inspection, accumulate, and multithread components. TraceSession.cancel() has no supported replacement: bound jobs with timeoutMillis or terminate the hosting process as the runner contract describes. TraceResult maps to TraceOutcome. PersistentGuestSession maps to BatchTracer (reusable guests only through batch). new BatchTraceService(w, m) maps to BatchTracer.builder().workers(w).maxJobsPerWorker(m).maxInFlight(Math.max(16, 2 * w)).build(), which keeps 3.x admission and submission order. findings.title: Reusable-guest lifetime is documented in Javadoc but not Markdown contracts
findings.quote: Each worker runs one job at a time in its own guest JVM. Single-stack jobs reuse guests and recycle them after the configured number of jobs. Multithread jobs use a fresh JVM so normal non-daemon thread lifetime applies

findings.original_problem:
Single-stack batch jobs (and one-shot Java Tracer.trace, which uses the same reusable-guest worker) do not follow normal JVM lifetime rules, and the same program gets a different result than `trace --result-envelope`.

1. When main returns, the harness interrupts any job thread still running, waits 250 ms, and then terminates the guest.
   - A valid program whose non-daemon worker finishes after main is reported `completed`, but its output silently changes ("worker interrupted" instead of "worker done").
   - A thread that never ends yields `failed`/`guest_exit` after about 0.5 s; the CLI reports `stopped`/`timeout`.
2. `System.exit(0)` yields `failed`/`guest_exit` in batch but `completed` in the CLI envelope.

The only hints are:
- batch.md's remark that multithread jobs get "normal non-daemon thread lifetime", which a reader must invert to infer anything.
- BOUNDED_TRACING's guest_exit row ("Nonzero dedicated-guest exit, or unexpected reusable-guest termination"). It describes a deliberate harness termination and a zero exit as "unexpected".

Grading integrators moving from the CLI to batch or Java get misclassified or silently altered results.
findings.original_fix:
Add a reference subsection to batch.md, "Single-stack jobs in a reusable guest", and link it from java-api.md (one-shot Tracer.trace), BOUNDED_TRACING's guest_exit row, and batch-jobs.md:56. It should state:
- After main returns, remaining job threads are interrupted, given about 250 ms, and the guest is then terminated. The job reports guest_exit, and output from interrupted threads changes.
- Any System.exit (including 0) ends the reusable guest and reports failed/guest_exit.
- Only multithread jobs (dedicated guest) and CLI trace keep normal non-daemon lifetime.

Reword the guest_exit row in BOUNDED_TRACING to describe these cases without "unexpected". Add a troubleshooting row ("batch reports guest_exit for a program that calls System.exit or starts threads"). Define dedicated and reusable guests once in GLOSSARY.md, reconciling "persistent guest" (GLOSSARY.md:95, java-api.md:236) with "reusable/reused guest" (BOUNDED_TRACING, batch.md, output.md).

findings.original_problem:
Consecutive single-stack jobs on a worker share one JVM. Between jobs the harness restores only:
- system properties
- default locales
- the default time zone
- the standard streams
- the default uncaught-exception handler

Other JDK-global state set by one job is visible to the next and changes its output, still with status `completed`.

The docs imply independence:
- The executable help reproduced in cli.md says "Execute independent trace jobs".
- batch-jobs.md lists source, output, observations, and snapshots as job-owned and mentions reuse only as an OS-isolation caveat.

No page says what is reset, what persists, or that `--max-jobs-per-worker 1` gives each job a fresh JVM. A grading integrator processing trusted submissions in one stream can get results that depend on the previous submission.

- Submitted classes load in a fresh class loader per job.
- Exactly what is restored (list from GuestHarness.cleanState).
- Other JVM-global state (JDK static configuration such as CookieHandler or logging settings, and files the guest writes) can persist into later jobs on the same worker until it is recycled.
- Use `--max-jobs-per-worker 1` / `BatchTracer.builder().maxJobsPerWorker(1)` when results must not depend on earlier jobs.
- The runner-contract rule of one process per job for untrusted input still applies.

Reword the batch-trace description in App.java:493 so it does not claim independence (for example, "separately correlated"), then regenerate cli.md.

findings.title: Batch silently ignores unknown or misspelled request and limit keys; limit key names never listed
findings.quote: | `limits` | Envelope limits using camelCase names; omitted limits are unlimited. |
findings.problem:
The batch parser silently ignores unknown or misspelled request properties and `limits` keys, with no diagnostic, and the docs never say so.

- The JSON limit names are never tabulated. batch.md says "camelCase names". BOUNDED_TRACING points to "the camelCase names from `TraceLimits`" (a Java type) and names only threads/frames/snapshotBytes, inside its Verification section. The limits table there lists only CLI options.
- A reader who writes `timeoutMs` (by analogy with `--timeout-ms`) or `maxSnapshots` gets an unlimited job, because omitted limits are unlimited.
- Case typos such as `multiThread` or `allbreakpoints` are also dropped, silently changing capture.
- An invalid limit value (negative) becomes `parse_error` with a null id, not the documented id-retaining `validation_error`, so it cannot be correlated under `--completion-order`.

Nothing tells integrators to check the echoed `result.limits`.

findings.original_problem:
The batch parser silently ignores unknown or misspelled request properties and `limits` keys, with no diagnostic, and the docs never say so.

- The JSON limit names are never tabulated. batch.md says "camelCase names". BOUNDED_TRACING points to "the camelCase names from `TraceLimits`" (a Java type) and names only threads/frames/snapshotBytes, inside its Verification section. The limits table there lists only CLI options.
- A reader who writes `timeoutMs` (by analogy with `--timeout-ms`) or `maxSnapshots` gets an unlimited job, because omitted limits are unlimited.
- Case typos such as `multiThread` or `allbreakpoints` are also dropped, silently changing capture.
- An invalid limit value (negative) becomes `parse_error` with a null id, not the documented id-retaining `validation_error`, so it cannot be correlated under `--completion-order`.

Nothing tells integrators to check the echoed `result.limits`.
findings.original_fix: In batch.md, add a `limits` key table mapping each CLI option to its JSON key and unit. State that unknown or misspelled request and limit properties are ignored without a diagnostic, and that omitted keys are unlimited. Tell clients to compare the response's `result.limits` with the intended budgets. Document that invalid limit values produce `parse_error` with a null `id`.

adjudications.rationale: Silently ignored protection keys combined with unlimited omitted budgets form a serious unsafe configuration contract. The reference gives no complete JSON-key map, and timeoutMillis/snapshots cannot be derived reliably from --timeout-ms/--max-snapshots; a plausible request can therefore run without intended protection and without any diagnostic. The negative-limit null-id correlation behavior is an additional correctness issue. External whole-job controls remain mandatory, but they do not make the promised per-job budget configuration reliable.

findings.title: No page explains how an uncaught guest exception appears; 'inspect the trace's events' cannot detect it
findings.quote: An ordinary trace can still record an exception thrown by the guest program. | Inspect the trace's events and guest output; exit status alone does not establish that the submitted program behaved correctly.
findings.problem: In single-thread capture (both formats), every snapshot's `event` is `step_line`. A program whose main throws gets no exception event and no main-exit capture. The default capture, which this page and trace-model.md:75-76 call the "Final main-exit state", instead returns the stop at the throwing line, and the exception is visible only as text in guest `stderr`. Instructors teaching exceptions cannot interpret this result from the docs. Integrators who follow the advice to inspect events would never detect an exception.

evidence.detail: `.event("step_line")` is hard-coded for every Python Tutor step.
The modern event falls back to "step_line" unless the snapshot carries an event. Only ThreadCapture.java:76-79 (multithread capture) sets "exception" or "main_exit".

evidence.ref: java -jar code-tracer.jar trace -i Boom.java --format modern  (main line 7 calls divide(1, 0); divide line 3 is `return a / b;`)
evidence.detail: Exit 0. One step: event step_line, line 3, method divide, callStack [main, divide], stderr "Exception in thread \"main\" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero ...". With --all-breakpoints the steps are step_line at lines 6, 7 and 3, with no main-exit capture. Python Tutor output has the same events and no exception_msg.
Exit 1, status failed, stopReason guest_exception, diagnostics ["java.lang.ArithmeticException"]. Only the envelope reports the exception as structured data.
"With no selected breakpoints or chronological option, ordinary tracing captures the main-exit state." This is not what happens when main throws.
